                                       Air Force conclusions for the ten years 1 ot UFO sightings
                                  involving approximately 5,700 reports were: Firstl there is no
                                  evidence thet the "u."lkno~..tns u were inimical or host1le; second,
                                  there is no evidence that these ~'unknowns u were inte::"ple.netary
           ·.                     spac;e ships; third, there is no evidence that these ''UnknCY..tns"
                                  represented technological developments or principles outside the
                                  range of our present day scientific knowledge; fourth, there is
                                  no evidence that these 11 ur.knowns n were a threat to the security
                                  or the country; end finally there was no physical or material
                                  evidence, net even a minute fragment, of' a so-called "flying
                                  saucer 11 was ever round..                                        -..._..~

      •        •            •                                                                                             · ANALYSIS
                          Was this a real "unknown"? A true unknown is an object ttiat remains u!l-
                       known after being seen under conditions which ~h.ould norm~lly ma_k~ the obJect
                       easily identifiable. · In order to satisfy this def1mtion c.erta1n conditions must be
                       present in a sighting:                              .   .                ·
                                                                                                                                                                                           •          ,                      .
                                     (1) The object should be · seen against a familiar _background suc_h as trees •
                                         . houses. nearby hills or low clouds. There 1s no way to est,mate the true
                                                 size of an object seen in a cloudless sky. A small object close to the
                                         observer may appear to be large and far away. When the dis~':'-ce or the
                                         object is fairly certain. the observer will not make a great mlSJudgment
                                         in the size.
                                     (2) The object must be faii·ly close to the observer. _For inst_a!lce. a balloon
                                         seen from a distance of two miles cannot be read1ly idenb£1ed, but a bal-
                                         loon that" is 200 feet away ~an be recognized immediately.
                                     (3) The duration of the sighting must be such that the observ~r has time ~nough
                                         to focus his eyes and observe the details oC the construc:tlon of the obJect.
                                         A sighting that lasts five seconds is highly questionable. The witness
                                         would have to be a very well trained observer to catch any detail in such
                                         a short time.
                                     (4) The object should maneuver in a manner that clearly distinguishes lt !rom
                                         a..coa.ventionat aircraft-or balloon• . Fo~ instance,..~ abrupt 90 o.r 180 degree •
                                     - · turns  would mark a true unknown. simply because no conventional object
                                         today could perform such maneuvers without structural failure •
                                 •
                   •     ·In the Fitzge:-ald sighting the first and second conditions are fulfilled completely•
 •                   The witness was in a very favorable position to observe the object because it was so
                     near. When the object was stationary in the adjacent lot. the witness was looking
                     down on it. The object was silhouetted against a familiar background. There was
                   . no chance for any sizable error in the estimated size of the object because its dis-
                     tance from the obs~rver was so accurately known. Even though the object was not
                     illuminated when:.-: was closest to t.'"le witness .. she could easily have seen any mark-
                     ings or protrusioc.s.                                   ·
                          The sighting lasted about 36 seconds • . This is enough time for a person to get
                     his bearings and focus his eye!\ even during su::h a startling experience. Mrs.
                     Fitzgerald had eno~.:gh time to get a. good look at the object. She ·could hardly have
                     been looking at, say, a fallen weather balloon in her yard for 36 seconds without
                     recognizing it for what it was. Her eyes might have been blurred at the beginning
                     or the sighting but_sufficient time passed for them to focus properly. Her descrip-
                     tion of the motions of the object would not be affected by a momentary lack of focus.
                     The image of the object remained so vivid in her mind that she was later able to
                     direct an artist in drawing it.           .        .
                          When the sequence of motions of the object is studied. it becomes obvious that
                     an "unnatural" phenomenon was observed. The object glided down in a northerly
                     direction, hovered. glided up in a southerly direction, made two quick turns and ·
                     then went straight up.                                         ·
           •
                          We must conclude that t!'!~ obj~ct was a genuine unknown. The nat~re or the ob-
                    _ject seen by l'.!rs. Fitzgerald must for the time bein~ remain a mystery. However,
                     some interesting observations can be made on the description of the appearance
                     and motions of the object.        .
      •
                          Altho~,tgh no marks of construction were seen on the object, the shape strongly •
                     suggests that it was manufactured. This is emphasized by tile pipes in the rim.
                     The general shape was symmetrical - - not the sxmmetry found in nature, but the
                     symmetry of a potter's wheel or lathe. The motions of the object can quite reason-
                     ~bly be considered as having been intelligently directed. Certainly they are not the
                     motions ~f an object caug.ht in the wind.                             .

                    WAS TinS A HOAX?                                                                    •                                                                                                      •
                        Mrs. Fitzgerald had nothing to gain. by reporting this sighting. To date she
                    has received nothing for her efforts but a scoffing from some of her neighbors;
                    while. on the other hand. she has the indirect support of the other people in her
                    neighborhood whose experiences are recorded in this report. These people were
    •               aU strangers to Mrs. Fitzgerald before the incident • .Mr. and Mrs. Fitzgerald
                    have volunteered to submit to a lie detector examination if any serious questioning
                    of their honesty is made.                        ·

                     WAS THIS A HALLUCINATION?
            •
                         'The fact that her son J'ohn also saw the object rules out the possibility that
                     the sig~ting was a hallucination•

                  WAS THIS OBJECT A GOVERNMENT .1-IISSII·E OR FLYING DEVICE?
                      No simple acswer to this question is possible •. The u.S. Government has
                  repeatedly denied that the UFO reports are being caused by government-operated
                  craft of any sort. Mrs. Fitzgerald reported no markings which would indicate           .... .
                  that the object was a u.s. device.
                      To answer this question more fully it is important to know that UFOs have
                  been. seen in every country. even behind the Iron Curtain. They have also flown
                  dangerousl;y close to commercial airlanes and over highly-restricted areas of
                  this country where an fiyiug is prohibited.                                   .
                      I! the United States had in its possession a device capable or the performance   •


                  attributed to the UFO. it would certainly not risk flying the device over foreign
                · countries. The same can also be said of all other powers on this planet. To have
                  a "saucer" crash or be forced down in a foreign land would naturally be most in-
                  jurious to the manufacturing power.. .      .
                   . ·No governm~nt tests are conducted over populated areas, and all military air-
                  craft are kept at a safe distance from commercial air lanes. The threatening
                  danger to the ci~~an population is enormous in both cases. It does not seem
                  reasonable that tl:.e government would jeopardize the safety of the public by flying
                  these devices whel"e they could do so much harm.
                      Fina]Jy, it see:n s strange that so many billions ot' dollars are being spent
                  yearly to perfect jet and rocket aircraft if we already have devices like the one
                  described by l'virs. Fitzgerald.

                                               ANALYSIS OF AIR FORCE CONCLUSION                                                                                                •

                             A railroad track runs 320 feet south of the Fitzgerald house~ At approximately
                     2:52a.m. a train left the Lorain station going east. Thi~ train probably_ passed
                     the Fitzgerald house a short time after 3. At the same time another tra1.n "!'as on
                     the tracks in the vicinity of Sheffield ~ake•. going w~st. T~e railroad offlc1als were
                      unable to furnish the time at which th1s tra1n passed the F1tzgerald house.
          •
                           The locomotives employ a special headlight called a m~rs g..       li ht11
                                                                                                      o~ a .. r;yralight''
                     which oscillates in a horizontal figure eight pattern. The light thro"!s 1ts beam over
                    · a much larger area than would be possible with a conve~tional head~1ght.                          ·
                         . If such a light did ·shine in the Fitzgerald b.edroom !flnd~w. it ~1ght have c.au~ed
                      the room to light up as Mrs. Fitzgerald descr1bed. W1th this in m1nd Mrs. F1tz
                      gerald and several members of the Committee observed trains approaching from
                      the east. At a distance the headlight beam is completely blocked by t~e houses ~nd
                      trees on the other side of the street. · When the train is near the headlight beam 1&
                      directed away from the house. Even on the extreme· swing of the beam the light
                      never hits the house.                          ·
                           At best this explanation. that Mrs. Fitzgerald was fooled by a train headlight.
                      could account only for the initial phase of the sighting in which she saw her room
                      brightly illuminated. It has no conceivable bearing·on the rest of her report. For
                      instance. how could she have mista..tc.en a train headlight for a solid object 22 feet
                      in diameter~ 6 feet high~ from a dis+~nce of only 10 feet away? And it should be
                      emphasized that the. witness lia.d her back to the railroad tracks during most of the
                      sighting.            .                       .                        .              .
                            As to the sout!d connected with t.."le object. it hardly seems possible that Mr~
                      Fitzgerald wot:ld not recognize the sound of a passing train. She has lived at her
                      present address since June of 1958, and has lived near railroads all of her life.
                      S~e has attempted to detect a simila!"ity between the sound she heard and the sound
                      or the trains, but has been unable to make any satisfactory connection.
                           The coast of I.ake Erie is about SOOO feet north of the Fitzgerald house. The
                      bouse is about 50 i eet above the level of the lake. Between the house and the lake
                      coast are a number of houses and t:-ees. The lake cannot be seen from the Fitz-
                      gerald house.                      .                     ·          ·
                           According to c;mer Boatswain 1\.Iate Schott of the Lorain Coast Guard station.
                       the patrol boat in question was never closer to the shore than one mile.                ·
                       . The spotli~ht on the type of boat used on this patrol is designed for s"otting bodies
                      or objects in the water near the boat. Consequently it has a very broad and diffused
                      beam. The beam fro:m this spotlight has no similarity to a searchlight beam of the
                     type used for spotting aircraft or for advertisil\g.                    ·                   · ;  ·
                           Therefore the light from this searchlight could hardly have been a factor in the
                      sighting or the object by Mrs. Fitzgerald; -                      .                 · .
                           The Air Force statement on this c:ase states: "Mrs. Steward (i. e.Stewart) of
                  · Lorain, a witness listed in Mrs. Fitzferald's report, could not recall anything unusual
                   · on the night of the reported sighting. •
      •
                           Mrs. Stewart has since signed a paper refuting this statement. (see Fig. 5)
                           It is interesting to note that the Air Force investigating team who visited
                     Mrs. Fitzgerald insisted that their job was entirely one of fact-finding. They
                     said that they themselves did not make any conclusions on a case, and explained
                     that this was done by "highly qualified experts in Dayton." The last paragraph
                     of the letter from General Fish_er contradicts this statement made by the ~ergeants •
              •                                                                                                                                    •

                   dlSregard tor the facts. In the final analysis which follows it will be shown that the

                                                                                   ANALYSIS OF AIR FORCE INVESTIGATION
                            .
                                              ·         ~TEU·I.       ..     ~    TEC.H,       .
                            In our opinion the Air For e investigation oft ·s case was crim1nally mis-
                       handled The                              tw;
                                            investigator , )t.Sgt. Haistan· an - M.~gt. Hof, spent two days.
                       tn ·Lorain ."investigating" the sighting. Their investigation. like ~e ATIC analys1s.
                       ,as a disgrace to the u.S. Air Force,. and an insult to the Amer1can. publlc whom
                       the Air Force supposedly represents.         .                  .
                                 Following is a list or the blunders committed by Sergeants Hof and Haistan:
                                 (1) They did not bother to observe the headlights on the trains passing near the
                         Fitzgerald house. This was despite the fact that th:y we~e ~equested t~ do so by a
                         member of the Committee present at the time they 1nterv1ewed Mrs. F1tzgerald. In
                         fact, this pOint was brought out in the presence of Mrs. Fitzgerald, an_d she stated
                         then that the headlight beam never. at any time, comes through her w1n~ow. The.
                         failure to make even this simple check on what was supposed to be a maJ~r factor .1n
                         the sighting is inexcusable and displays the grossest inefficiency.
                              (2) The presence of any sort o! lake activity should not have been listed as a        •
                        factor· in the s i ghting. At the closest point to the Fitzgerald house .t he lake is 3000
                        feet away... It is impossmle to see the la..lte from the Fitzgerald house. This was ex ..
                        ·p tained to- Sgt. Hof by a member or the Committee at the time the sergeant was in the
                        front yard of the Fitzgerald house. The sergeant was asked to explain how. since              ·
                        according to their investigation the weather was bad at the time of the sighting, any ·
                         light could have been seen reflected from off the clouds, or how light in any other man-
                       ·ner could have reached the Fitzgeral d house !rom the lake. Sergeant Hof acknowledged
                         these objections b~t made no attem?t to answer them.
                              (3) General Fisher's letter states that Chief Schott rer.orted he was using his spot-
                         light "in an attempt to attract the at tention of another ship •. and that the light was dir-
                       ·ected toward shore "in the general direction of Mrs. Fitzgerald's house. 11 If the ser-
                         geants had made a conscientious check with Chief Schott they would have noted that at
                         the time he _was usir.g tile light to attract ano~her ship he was at a place on the lake
                       4t    miles from the F itzgerald house. They would also have noted that the spotlight
                        beam would have had to travel through downtown Lorain on its way to the house•. As
                         mentioned in the analysis of the Air Force Conclusion, the sergeants apparently did
                         not know that the Coast Guard boat had a light which could not be focused on clouds in
                        the manner of a sear-chlight. Chief' Schott has signed a statement specifying his posi-
                        tion and activities on the morning of September 21.            .     ..
                              (4) How the sergeants could ma.ke the statement that Mrs. Stewart "could not
                         recall anything unusual" is indeed difficult to understand. Mrs. Stewart•s signed
                        statement (Fig. 5) is definite proof that this was either a deliberate attempt to
                        distort the facts, a:o. unforgivable act of negligence. or else an extreme case of
                        ignorance.                ·
                              (5) How the sergeants could make the ·statement that Mr. Grego or Lorain,
                        another witness, "was not available for interview", is even more pathetic in view of
                         the !act that the witness referred to in Mrs. Fitzgerald's summary to ATIC was
                        actually MRS. Greg.:l.                               -                            .
                        . (6) General Fisher's statement reads, "The weather at the time or the incident
                        was a misty rain with haze and smoke." The sergeants apparently discovered this
                        through th,e same mental process which led them to conclude that Mrs. Stewart
          •             could remember seeing nothing. The weather at the time of the sighting. as des-
                        cribed by the witness verbally and in writing in the Air Force' report form, was
                        not raini~?-g. There is no reason to suppose that th,.e witness was mistaken on this
                        point. ·        .
      -                  . As to .the. presence or Jimoke. this undoubtedly refers to the fact that the U.S.

        Steel Company has a plant about .1 j miles SW or the house. U~ortunately. the. ser- ·
         geants failed to check the wind direction at the time of the sighting. Had they done
         ao they would have discovered that smoke from the steel plant could not have blown
        toward the Fitzgerald house berore 4:00a.m. on September 21. It can be assumed.
        however, that there was some haze during the sighting, but the· effect this would
         have on the viewing o! such a large object at a range ·of 10 to 50 feet is.not made
         clear in General Fisher's Statement.
              The statement concerning the weather not only has little foundation in fact. but
        ·i s written in a manner calculated to discredit the sighting. It is somewhat surpris-
         ing that the report does not also include accounts of tornadoes and blizzards con-
         verging over Sheffield Lake at the time of the sighting.                ·
              (7)The sergeants made several omissio_n s. indicating they_had little or no in-
         tenti~n or making an honest investigation of this sighting. (a) They did not make a
         house to house check in the neighborhood for supplementary. evidence. (b) They
         did not ask Mrs. Fitzgerald to make a 3-dimensional drawing of the object. The
         sergeants showed almost no interest in the shape of the object, which actually
         should have been the most important point in their entire report. (c) They showed
         almost no interest in the motions o! the object, and relied upon a member of the
         Committee to expWn the motions to them. Here again, the maneuvers of the ob-
         ject should have been the second most important point of the official report. (d) Mrs.
         Fitzgerald was made to fill out the standard Air Force UFO reporting form. This
         form was designed to report objects seen in the sky, no~ on the grqunci_ Mrs. Fitz.- .
         gerald said that it was very difficult for her to convey in this report the idea that she .
         had seen a large~ solid object moving in her front yard• . The sergeants did not take
         notes during their interview with Mrs. Fitzgerald; consequently. the report form
        .must t?e the only of!icial record of her sighting.


             The investigat!.o!l and analysis of this case by the u.s. Air Force is typical of
        the treatment which has been given LTO reports over the past ten years. This case
        has now become one or the 98. lo/o of all UFO reports which the Air Force terms as
        "known".                                                               ·
             The figure of 98.1~ was rele.ased on October 6, 1958 in news release number
        986-58. T.h e release goes on to say. ' 1 Refinernents in investigative procedure have
        resulted in a steady decline of unknowns." After studyi nK the Fitzgerald report it
        should be manifestly clear what the Air Force means by refinements in invest-
        igative procedure".                                                                                         .
             In a letter to a member of the UFO Research Committee, General Fisher said,                                                                                    .   .
        "The Air Force is ·interested in the truth concerning reported sightings and is com-
        pelled to deal scientiiically and objectively with facts. We feel sure our analyses
        and evaluations by qu.alif'ied scientific personnel of the reported sightings of unident-
        ified flying objects are more than adequate."                                                             ·
    •
             This is an example of the duplicity which has characterized the Air Force treat-
        ment of the UFO problem.                       .
             The Committee believes that the complete disregard of !acts, which the Air Force
•       has consistently exhibited through the ·years wherever the UFO is concerned, should
        be halted immediately. The public must be given the truth regarding the existence
        of these objects. We suggest that others who similarly feel that the UFO problem
        {s being gravely mishandled write their representatives in congress, and request an
        investigation of the Air Force UFO project.
